# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero. On tidally locked exoplanets like those around TRAPPIST-1, this contrast fundamentally shapes atmospheric behavior.

Rather than destroying climates entirely, tidal locking often generates remarkable stabilizing mechanisms. On planets with substantial atmospheres, powerful winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures on both sides. Climate models suggest that on some tidally locked worlds, a massive permanent storm forms at the substellar point—the region receiving direct starlight—while the nightside accumulates vast ice sheets. Crucially, if atmospheric circulation weakens, these ice sheets could grow so thick that they trap the planet's entire water inventory on the dark side, a scenario called "airless" or "eye" planets.

Ocean circulation provides another moderating force. A planet with a global ocean can distribute heat efficiently, potentially maintaining a habitable ring between the scorched dayside and frozen nights
